---
title: "Performance"
---

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)

dir <- "performance"
startup <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "startup.csv"))
calls <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "calls.csv"))
versions <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "versions.csv"))

interfaces <- c("jlbind", "JuliaCall", "JuliaConnectoR")
colors <- c(
  jlbind = "#2a78d6",
  JuliaCall = "#eb6834",
  JuliaConnectoR = "#1baf7a"
)

# Format a time in seconds with a sensible unit.
fmt_time <- function(s) {
  ifelse(
    s < 1e-3,
    sprintf("%.3g µs", s * 1e6),
    ifelse(s < 1, sprintf("%.3g ms", s * 1e3), sprintf("%.3g s", s))
  )
}

startup_med <- tapply(startup$seconds, startup$interface, median)[interfaces]
greet <- calls[calls$task == "greet", ]
greet_med <- setNames(greet$median, greet$interface)[interfaces]
shift <- calls[calls$task == "shift", ]
shift_at <- function(n) {
  setNames(shift$median[shift$n == n], shift$interface[shift$n == n])[
    interfaces
  ]
}
```

jlbind calls Julia code that was compiled ahead of time, through one `.Call()`
per function. The alternatives,
[JuliaCall](https://github.com/JuliaInterop/JuliaCall) and
[JuliaConnectoR](https://github.com/stefan-m-lenz/JuliaConnectoR), run Julia
itself: JuliaCall embeds a Julia session in the R process, and JuliaConnectoR
starts one in a separate process and talks to it over a socket. This article
compares the three on the same Julia functions.

In short, on this machine, jlbind is ready to use
`r round(startup_med[["JuliaConnectoR"]] / startup_med[["jlbind"]])` to
`r round(startup_med[["JuliaCall"]] / startup_med[["jlbind"]])` times sooner,
and a call costs `r fmt_time(greet_med[["jlbind"]])` rather than
`r fmt_time(greet_med[["JuliaCall"]])` (JuliaCall) or
`r fmt_time(greet_med[["JuliaConnectoR"]])` (JuliaConnectoR).

## The benchmarks

The functions are the same as in the `hellojl` test client in jlbind's
repository:

```julia
greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64) = x .+ by
```

jlbind calls them through `hellojl`, compiled into a jlbind library. JuliaCall
and JuliaConnectoR evaluate the same definitions and call them with
`julia_call()` and `juliaFun()`. Each interface runs in fresh R processes, since
jlbind and JuliaCall can't share one.

- **Startup**: the time from loading the package to the result of the first
  call, `greet("world")`, in a new R process (R's own startup excluded),
  repeated `r max(startup$rep)` times.
- **Call overhead**: the median time of `greet("world")`, a string in and a
  string out, after the first call.
- **Data transfer**: the median time of `shift(x, 1)` for numeric vectors `x` of
  length 10 to 10^7^, which copies `x` to Julia and the result back.

The benchmark script is
[`vignettes/articles/performance/benchmark.R`](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/jlbind/blob/main/vignettes/articles/performance/benchmark.R).
The results below were run on:

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(versions, col.names = c("", ""))
```

## Startup

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Interface = interfaces,
    Median = fmt_time(startup_med),
    Min = fmt_time(tapply(startup$seconds, startup$interface, min)[interfaces]),
    Max = fmt_time(tapply(startup$seconds, startup$interface, max)[interfaces])
  ),
  align = "lrrr",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

For jlbind, startup is loading the compiled library and binding the package's
routines. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR start Julia, and compile each function
the first time it is called. With a real Julia package instead of two one-line
functions, compiling and loading the package typically take much longer than
here.

## Call overhead

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Interface = interfaces,
    `Time per call` = fmt_time(greet_med),
    `Relative to jlbind` = sprintf("%.0f×", greet_med / greet_med[["jlbind"]]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrr",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A jlbind call is a `.Call()` into the compiled library, where the arguments are
converted with R's C API and the function is called directly. JuliaCall converts
arguments and looks up the function at run time in the embedded session.
JuliaConnectoR serializes the call to a separate Julia process and the result
back, so each call costs a round trip.

## Data transfer

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Median time of shift(x, 1) against the length of x, on log scales, for
#|   jlbind, JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR. jlbind is fastest at every length.

shift$interface <- factor(shift$interface, levels = interfaces)
starts <- shift[shift$n == min(shift$n), ]

ggplot(shift, aes(n, median, color = interface)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 1) +
  geom_text(
    data = starts,
    aes(label = interface),
    hjust = 1,
    nudge_x = -0.12,
    size = 3.5,
    color = "#52514e"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = 10^(1:7),
    labels = scales::label_math(10^.x, format = log10),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.3, 0.03))
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = 10^(-6:0), labels = fmt_time) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors) +
  labs(x = "Length of x", y = "Median time of shift(x, 1)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e8e7e3", linewidth = 0.3),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#52514e"),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "#52514e")
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

wide <- reshape(
  shift[c("interface", "n", "median")],
  idvar = "n",
  timevar = "interface",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(wide) <- sub("median.", "", names(wide), fixed = TRUE)
wide[interfaces] <- lapply(wide[interfaces], fmt_time)
wide$n <- format(wide$n, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  wide,
  col.names = c("Length", interfaces),
  align = "rrrr",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```
